l: agriculture, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Agriculture is central to the interpretation of Ceres as a goddess of the Earth and corn. Ceres is said to have taught her subjects to till the ground and sow corn, while the return of crops allegorically explains Jupiter’s settlement of the dispute between Ceres and Pluto.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres searches throughout the earth for Proserpine and learns from Arethusa that Proserpine is in the world of darkness as the powerful spouse of the Infernal King. Ceres appeals to Jupiter, who permits Proserpine to return to heaven only if she has eaten no food there. Because Proserpine has eaten seven pomegranate seeds, Ascalaphus prevents her return and Proserpine changes him into an owl. The Sirens receive wings so they can search more swiftly for Proserpine.

l: Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres searches through the lands and seas for Proserpine and learns from Arethusa that her daughter is in the world of darkness. In her grief and anger, she damages the agriculture of Sicily, then appeals to Jupiter to restore Proserpine.

l: Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Proserpine is seen by Arethusa in the world of darkness, where she is sad but already a queen and the powerful spouse of the Infernal King. She has eaten seven grains from a pomegranate, which prevents her complete return to heaven, and she changes Ascalaphus into an owl.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter receives Ceres’s appeal and says that Proserpine is a charge shared by him and Ceres. He agrees that Proserpine may return to heaven if she has touched no food in the Infernal Regions.

l: Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pluto is identified with the ravisher whose dominions contain Proserpine and with her husband in the Infernal Regions.

l: Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Arethusa, the Alpheian Nymph, tells Ceres that Sicily did not willingly provide a path for Proserpine’s abduction. She explains that, while traveling beneath the earth, she saw Proserpine in the Stygian stream’s vicinity, already a queen and the spouse of the Infernal King.

l: Ascalaphus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ascalaphus sees Proserpine eat seven grains of a pomegranate and reveals this fact, preventing her return. Proserpine punishes him by transforming him into an owl.

l: Sicily, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Sicily is the place where Ceres finds evidence of Proserpine’s loss and where Arethusa now dwells. Ceres angrily breaks the ploughs there, kills the husbandmen and oxen, and causes the land’s fertility to fail.

l: world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Earth is searched throughout by Ceres, but it is too limited to contain her search. Its fertility is damaged when Ceres causes the land to deny the return of what has been deposited in it.

l: Infernal Regions, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Infernal Regions are the domain where Proserpine has been carried and where she is the queen and spouse of the Infernal King. Jupiter’s condition for her return concerns whether she has eaten food there.

l: Proserpine’s girdle, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Proserpine’s girdle has fallen into the sacred stream at Cyane. Cyane points it out on the surface of the water, and Ceres recognizes it.

l: pomegranate, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: A pomegranate grows on a bending tree in a finely cultivated garden. Proserpine plucks it and eats seven grains from its pale rind.

l: pomegranate seeds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Proserpine eats seven pomegranate seeds while walking in the garden. Their consumption prevents her complete return to heaven under the law of the Destinies.

l: owl, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The owl is the form into which Proserpine changes Ascalaphus. It is described as a tawny-winged, obscene bird that foretells approaching woe and is a direful omen to mortals.

l: agriculture and fertility, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres’s anger causes the fertility of Sicily to be ruined. Corn dies, seed is spoiled, and heat, rain, winds, constellations, birds, darnel, thistles, and weeds damage the crops.

l: abduction of Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Proserpine’s abduction is revealed to Ceres through the girdle found at Cyane and Arethusa’s account of seeing Proserpine in the world of darkness. Ceres calls the act an outrage and asks Jupiter to have her daughter restored.

l: Ceres's search for Proserpina, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres searches through the whole earth and across the seas, finding no immediate answer. Her search brings her to Sicily, where Cyane’s girdle and Arethusa’s testimony reveal Proserpine’s location.

l: Proserpine’s return to the upper world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter agrees that Proserpine may return to heaven if she has eaten no food in the Infernal Regions. Her eating of seven pomegranate seeds prevents the return permitted by that condition.

l: Ascalaphus’s punishment and transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: For revealing that Proserpine ate pomegranate seeds, Ascalaphus is punished by Proserpine. His head becomes a beak, feathers, and large eyes; his body is covered with tawny wings, and he becomes a sluggish owl.

l: the law of the Destinies, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The law of the Destinies provides that Proserpine may return only if she has touched no food in the Infernal Regions. Because she has eaten pomegranate seeds, the condition is not fulfilled.

l: the pomegranate eating, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: While walking innocently in a cultivated garden, Proserpine plucks a pomegranate and chews seven grains from it. Ascalaphus witnesses the act and reports it, preventing her return to heaven.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the notes surrounding the abduction of Proserpine, including Ceres's search and Arethusa's account of what happened. It discusses Proserpine's girdle, the pomegranate seeds that bound her to the Infernal Regions, and Ascalaphus's punishment and transformation. It also describes the Sirens' proposed search for Proserpine and gives explanations for several elements of the myth. Apollodorus's version of the treaty assigns Proserpine nine months with Ceres and three with Pluto, while other writers divide the time equally.

l: Proserpine’s girdle, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The girdle was worn by both sexes to fasten and raise the tunic, and it could also hold money or a purse. Proserpine's continued wearing of her girdle is treated as evidence of the violence committed against her, since young women discontinued wearing it on their wedding day.

l: Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Proserpine was carried away by Pluto, and the condition of her girdle revealed that she had been violently abducted. After eating pomegranate seeds, she was required to spend part of the year with Pluto in the Infernal Regions and the remainder with Ceres on earth.

l: Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Arethusa discovered and reported to Ceres what had happened to Proserpine. Ovid makes Arethusa the informant in this account, although in the Fourth Book of the Fasti he instead represents the Sun as giving Ceres the information.

l: Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ceres searched for Proserpine and learned from Arethusa that Pluto had carried her away. She was involved in the arrangement governing Proserpine's periods on earth and in the Infernal Regions.

l: Apollodorus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Apollodorus says that Proserpine stayed nine months with Ceres and three months with Pluto. He also describes Ascalaphus as the son of Acheron and the Nymph Orphne or Gorgyra, and says that Ceres placed a rock upon him before he was changed into an owl after being liberated by Hercules.

l: pomegranate, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Proserpine plucked and ate pomegranate seeds, which caused her to remain partly in the Infernal Regions. The Thesmophoriazusae therefore took special care not to taste the pomegranate during the rites of Ceres.

l: Ascalaphus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ascalaphus revealed that Proserpine had eaten pomegranate seeds and thereby hindered her complete restoration to Ceres. According to different accounts, Ceres punished him with a rock, and he was transformed into an owl or a lizard.

l: Infernal Regions, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Infernal Regions are also signified by names such as Avernus and are described as containing Phlegethon, a burning river. Proserpine was required to spend part of each year there with Pluto.

l: Sirens, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Sirens were said to be daughters of the river Acheloüs and one of the Muses. Ovid probably made them ask the Gods to change them into birds so that they could search for Proserpine.

l: Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pluto carried away Proserpine and took her to the Infernal Regions. He was reproached by the Nymph Cyane for his treatment of Proserpine and punished Ascalaphus according to some versions of the story.

l: treaty concerning Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The treaty concerning Proserpine required her to remain part of the year with Ceres on earth and part with Pluto in the Infernal Regions. Apollodorus assigns nine months to Ceres and three to Pluto, while other writers divide the time equally.

l: Ascalaphus’s punishment and transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ascalaphus's transformation is variously described as a change into an owl or into a lizard. The explanation connects the owl version with his death in Pluto's mines and the lizard version with the resemblance between his name and the Greek word for lizard.

l: Ceres's search for Proserpina, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ceres searched for Proserpine and received information about her from Arethusa. The Sirens were also said to have sought permission to become birds so that they could search for Proserpine, possibly reflecting a tradition that they equipped a ship for this purpose.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter settles the dispute between Ceres and Pluto by dividing the year between them, allowing Ceres's daughter to spend equal months with her mother and her husband. Ceres, relieved by her daughter's recovery, asks Arethusa why she became a sacred spring. Arethusa recounts how Alpheus pursued her across the country after finding her bathing, and how Diana hid and transformed her into a stream. Alpheus then changed into water and tried to mingle with her, but Diana carried Arethusa through underground passages to Ortygia.

l: Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres is satisfied with Jupiter's decision concerning her daughter and becomes joyful at recovering her. She asks Arethusa about the cause of her wanderings and why she is a sacred spring.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter mediates between Pluto and Ceres and divides the rolling year equally between them.

l: Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres's daughter becomes a common divinity of two kingdoms, spending equal months with her mother and with her husband.

l: Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Arethusa tells Ceres that she was an Achaian nymph who enjoyed hunting and was pursued by Alpheus while bathing. After Diana concealed her in a cloud, Arethusa changed into a stream and was carried underground to Ortygia.

l: Alpheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Alpheus sees Arethusa bathing and pursues her relentlessly across fields, mountains, and several regions. After Arethusa becomes a stream, he changes from mortal form into water so that he can mingle with her.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Diana responds to Arethusa's plea for aid by hiding her beneath a dense cloud. She then cleaves the ground and carries Arethusa through dark caverns to Ortygia.

l: the division of the year between Ceres and Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter divides the rolling year equally between Ceres and Pluto. Ceres's daughter consequently spends equal numbers of months with her mother and her husband.

l: the passion of Alpheus for Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Alpheus pursues Arethusa after she flees from the stream where she was bathing. He follows her over distant regions until Diana hides her, and he continues searching around the concealing cloud.

l: Arethusa's transformation into a fountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: While concealed and besieged by fear, Arethusa begins to shed water from her body, and wherever she steps a lake flows. She is changed into a stream, while Alpheus becomes water and attempts to mingle with her.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the myth of the river Alpheus and the fountain Arethusa, including their supposed connection between Elis and Sicily. It says that the Phoenicians named the Sicilian fountain “Alphaga” or “Arith,” while the Greeks later misunderstood these names and linked the fountain with their own river Alpheus. Poets developed this misunderstanding into the story of Alpheus’s love for the Nymph Arethusa and his pursuit of her across the sea. Although Pausanias regarded the tale as a fable, some ancient historians and the oracle of Delphi treated the connection between Alpheus and Arethusa as real.

l: Alpheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Alpheus is a river that rose in Arcadia, ran through the territory of the Eleans, and entered the sea near Cyllene. The Greeks associated it with the fountain Arethusa in Sicily, imagining that it crossed beneath the sea to reach her.

l: Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Arethusa is a Sicilian fountain surrounded by willows. In the poetic story, she is a Nymph pursued by the river god Alpheus, and the oracle of Delphi describes Alpheus as mixing his waters with her.

l: Fountain of Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Fountain of Arethusa was given names by the Phoenicians that meant “the fountain of the willows” or “a stream.” The Greeks misunderstood these names and used the similarity to the name Alpheus to explain the supposed connection between the fountain and the river.

l: Sicily, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Sicily was settled by Phoenicians and later visited by Greeks, whose misunderstanding of local names helped produce the story of Alpheus and Arethusa. The fountain of Arethusa was located there.

l: Phœnicians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Phoenicians settled in Sicily and named the fountain surrounded by willows “Alphaga,” meaning “the fountain of the willows,” or “Arith,” meaning “a stream.”

l: Greeks, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Greeks arrived in Sicily after the Phoenicians and did not understand the meanings of the names “Alphaga” and “Arith.” Remembering their own river Alpheus, they imagined that it had crossed the sea to Sicily.

l: the passion of Alpheus for Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The passion of Alpheus for Arethusa was a poetic story based on the similarity between the names of the river and the fountain. It describes Alpheus pursuing Arethusa across many countries and beneath the sea, though Pausanias regarded the story as a mere fable.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres sends Triptolemus in her chariot to scatter seeds and teach cultivation throughout the earth. In Scythia, King Lyncus envies Triptolemus and tries to kill him while he sleeps, but Ceres transforms Lyncus into a lynx. After the song is finished, the Nymphs declare that the Goddesses of Helicon have won the contest against the Emathian sisters. The Emathian sisters are punished for their abuse and transformed into magpies.

l: Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ceres yokes two dragons to her chariot and sends Triptolemus to scatter seeds in fallow and restored ground. When Lyncus attempts to kill Triptolemus, Ceres transforms him into a lynx.

l: Triptolemus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Triptolemus travels in Ceres's chariot over Europe, Asia, and the earth, carrying her gifts of seeds. In Scythia, he tells Lyncus that he comes from Athens to provide fruitful harvests and wholesome food.

l: Scythia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Scythia is the land where Lyncus is king. Triptolemus arrives there during his journey.

l: Lyncus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Lyncus, the king of Scythia, receives Triptolemus hospitably but envies him and attempts to kill him while he sleeps. Ceres changes him into a lynx.

l: lynx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The lynx is the form into which Ceres transforms Lyncus when he tries to attack Triptolemus.

l: song of Calliope, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Arethusa's account includes the story of Ceres, Triptolemus, and Lyncus. The greatest of the singers finishes her learned song before the Nymphs judge the contest.

l: Nymphs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Nymphs unanimously declare that the Goddesses of Helicon have won the contest. They witness the punishment of the defeated Emathian sisters.

l: Muses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Goddesses of Helicon are declared the conquerors of the contest by the Nymphs.

l: Emathian sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Emathian sisters are defeated, abuse their opponents, and despise the threatening language directed at them. As they try to speak and gesture, feathers grow from their nails, their arms become covered with feathers, their faces form hard beaks, and they become birds.

l: contest between the Muses and the Emathian sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The contest ends with the Nymphs declaring that the Goddesses of Helicon have won. The defeated Emathian sisters respond with abuse and are punished.

l: punishment of the Emathian sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Emathian sisters are transformed into birds after abusing the victors. Their punishment leaves them with their original talkativeness, jarring garrulity, and great love of chattering.

l: magpies, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The transformed Emathian sisters hang poised in the air as magpies, becoming the scandal of the groves. As magpies, they retain their talkativeness and love of chattering.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains Triptolemus's connection with Eleusis, the establishment and spread of the mysteries and worship of Ceres, and the possible links between these traditions and agriculture. It describes Triptolemus's voyages in a ship called a flying dragon and suggests that dangers during his travels inspired the story of Lyncus. It also discusses traditions concerning Proserpine, Pluto, Erectheus, and the war between the Eleusinians and Athenians. Eumolpus and Erectheus were both killed in battle, after which their descendants received different religious and political offices.

l: Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ceres's mysteries were established at Eleusis, and Triptolemus was said to have been nursed by her milk and purified by fire. Triptolemus also introduced her worship into different countries.

l: Triptolemus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Triptolemus reigned at Eleusis when the mysteries of Ceres were established there. He carried corn to different countries by ship and introduced the worship of Ceres, whose priest he was; traditions also said that Ceres nursed and purified him.

l: Eleusis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Eleusis was the place where Triptolemus reigned and where the mysteries of Ceres were established. It was also associated with the Eleusinians and with Eumolpus's religious office.

l: Eleusinian mysteries, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The mysteries of Ceres were established at Eleusis during the reign of Triptolemus. The unit suggests that they were probably connected with the introduction of Ceres's mysterious worship, which may have been imported from Egypt.

l: worship of Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Triptolemus carried the worship of Ceres to different countries during his voyages. The unit identifies this spread of worship as a likely subject of the story about Triptolemus being nursed and purified by Ceres.

l: agriculture, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Some have connected the story with the introduction of agriculture into Greece. The unit considers it more probable that the story concerns the introduction of Ceres's worship, while allowing that improved methods of tilling the ground may also have been learned from Egypt.

l: Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit says that the worship of Ceres was probably introduced into Greece from Egypt. It also mentions the possibility that Greece learned improved methods of tilling the ground through intercourse with Egypt.

l: Erectheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Erectheus was king of Athens and fought against the Eleusinians. He was told by an oracle that he would win if he sacrificed his daughter Proserpine, and he and Eumolpus were later killed in battle.

l: Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Proserpine was the daughter of Erectheus. An oracle reportedly told Erectheus to sacrifice her in order to be victorious.

l: Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pluto is associated with the story of the rape of Proserpine. The unit suggests that Erectheus's oracle and the required sacrifice of Proserpine may have helped give rise to that story.

l: rape of Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The story of the rape of Proserpine by Pluto may have been partly inspired by the tradition that Erectheus was told to sacrifice his daughter Proserpine.

l: Greeks, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The first Greeks initiated into the mysteries of Ceres were, according to a fragment of Homer cited by Pausanias, Celeus, Triptolemus, Eumolpus, and Diocles. Clement of Alexandria gives a partly different list.

l: Eumolpus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Eumolpus was identified as one of the first Greeks initiated into the mysteries of Ceres. He was the Hierophant, made war against Erectheus, and was killed in battle; afterward, his descendants retained the office of Hierophant.

l: Eleusinians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Eleusinians fought against Erectheus, king of Athens. Their conflict ended with Eumolpus and Erectheus being killed in battle.

l: Athens, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Athens was ruled by Erectheus, who was king there during the conflict with the Eleusinians. After the battle, the posterity of Erectheus was assigned the kingship of Athens.

l: Hierophant, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Hierophant was the explainer of the mysteries of Eleusis. Eumolpus held this office, and after his death it was retained by his descendants.

l: war between Eumolpus and Erectheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Eumolpus made war against Erectheus, king of Athens. The war ended with both of them being killed in battle, after which their descendants received separate hereditary roles.

l: battle between the Eleusinians and Athenians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The battle between the Eleusinians and Athenians resulted in the deaths of Eumolpus and Erectheus. It was then agreed that Erectheus's descendants would rule Athens and Eumolpus's descendants would retain the office of Hierophant.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SIXTH.
s: Arachne, a highly skilled weaver from a humble family, challenges Minerva to a contest after refusing to acknowledge that the goddess taught her art. Minerva and Arachne weave intricate scenes, with Arachne depicting the deceptive transformations and misdeeds of the gods. Although Minerva cannot fault Arachne’s workmanship, she becomes enraged, tears the web, and strikes Arachne. Arachne hangs herself, but Minerva saves her and transforms her into a spider, condemning her descendants to the same fate.

l: Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SIXTH.
s: Minerva hears of Arachne’s skill and challenges her after Arachne refuses to yield to the goddess. She disguises herself as an old woman to advise Arachne, then reveals her identity and competes with her. Enraged by Arachne’s successful depiction of the gods’ misdeeds, Minerva tears the web, strikes Arachne, and transforms her into a spider.

l: Arachne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SIXTH.
s: Arachne is the daughter of Idmon of Colophon and becomes renowned throughout Lydia for her exceptional skill in working wool. She challenges Minerva and produces a web depicting the transformations and deceptions of the gods. After Minerva strikes her, Arachne hangs herself, but Minerva takes pity on her and changes her form.

l: Arachne's transformation into a spider, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SIXTH.
s: After Arachne hangs herself, Minerva supports her and decrees that she and her descendants shall continue to hang. Minerva sprinkles her with a noxious Hecatean herb, causing her hair, nose, and ears to disappear, her body to become small, and her fingers to become legs. Arachne’s belly takes over the rest of her body, and she begins producing thread and weaving as a spider.

l: the weaving contest, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SIXTH.
s: Minerva and Arachne weave separate webs using fine warp, woof, shuttles, and vivid colors. Minerva depicts the contest between Neptune and herself for the city and adds examples of mortals punished for challenging the gods. Arachne depicts Europa and numerous divine transformations and deceptions, producing work that Minerva cannot blame for its craftsmanship.

l: the spider, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SIXTH.
s: The spider is the form Arachne assumes after Minerva’s transformation. It gives forth a thread and works at its web as Arachne had formerly worked at weaving.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the story of Arachne, a highly skilled Lydian artist who challenged Minerva in weaving and textile artistry. It summarizes the myths depicted in their works, including the dispute between Neptune and Minerva over the naming and patronage of Athens. It also discusses interpretations of Arachne’s alleged transformation and provides rationalizing explanations for several myths, including stories about the Pygmies. Ovid is identified as the poet who used Arachne’s contest to present numerous related fables.

l: Arachne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Arachne is described as the daughter of Idmon, a Lydian of low extraction, and as the most skilful artist of her time at working in silk and wool. She challenged Minerva and represented numerous myths in her work; according to the explanation, she later hanged herself in despair and was associated with the story of transformation into a spider.

l: Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Minerva is presented as Arachne’s divine rival in the contest of weaving. She was also credited by some with inventing linen cloths and nets, and her victory over Neptune was connected with the olive tree, agriculture, and the patronage of Athens.

l: Ovid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Ovid uses the contest between Arachne and Minerva to introduce and elaborate on several myths. He also mentions the Pygmies and their supposed continual warfare with the Cranes.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

s: Tereus unknowingly eats Itys’s remains at the banquet prepared by Progne. When he learns what has happened, he pursues Progne and Philomela with a drawn sword, but is transformed into an epops, or lapwing.

l: Itys, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Itys comes to his mother and shows her affection, but Progne decides to kill him because he resembles Tereus. Progne and Philomela murder him, mangle his body, cook it, and serve it to Tereus.

l: revenge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Revenge against Tereus drives Progne’s actions. She considers burning him, mutilating him, or killing him, and ultimately takes revenge by murdering Itys and feeding his remains to Tereus.

l: captivity of Philomela, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Philomela is held in a lonely dwelling after Tereus has violated her and cut out her tongue. Progne rescues her by breaking open the gates and bringing her to the court of Tereus.

l: the murder of Itys, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Progne and Philomela murder Itys in a remote part of the house. Progne strikes him with a sword, and Philomela cuts his throat; they then mangle and cook his body.

l: banquet of Itys, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Progne prepares a private banquet for Tereus and serves him the cooked remains of Itys. When Tereus asks for Itys, Progne tells him that what he seeks is within him, and Philomela throws Itys’s bloody head into his face.

l: the symbolic transformations of Philomela, Progne, and Tereus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: After Tereus pursues the sisters, Progne is transformed into a swallow and Philomela into a nightingale. Tereus is transformed into a crested bird with a long bill, the epops or lapwing.

l: epops, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The epops is the bird into which Tereus is transformed. It has a crested head, a prolonged bill in place of Tereus’s spear, and a face that appears armed.

l: the swallow, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Progne becomes a swallow while fleeing from Tereus.

l: the nightingale, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Philomela becomes a nightingale while fleeing from Tereus.

l: Philomela, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Philomela is described as being transformed into a nightingale in the principal account, where the bird’s concealment among woods and thickets represents the concealment of her misfortunes and sorrows. Anacreon and Apollodorus instead say that Philomela was changed into a swallow.

l: Progne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Progne is described as being transformed into a swallow, whose presence around human dwellings symbolizes her restless search for the son whom she has murdered in a frantic fit. Anacreon and Apollodorus reverse this account and say that Progne became a nightingale.

l: Tereus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Tereus is represented by the lapwing, a bird associated with filth and impurity, symbolizing his unscrupulous character. The lapwing’s slow flight also signifies that Tereus could not overtake Progne and Philomela.

l: the symbolic transformations of Philomela, Progne, and Tereus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The transformations are presented as symbolic depictions of the characters’ different natures and actions. The principal account associates Tereus with the lapwing, Philomela with the nightingale, and Progne with the swallow, although Anacreon and Apollodorus reverse the transformations of the two women.

l: the murder of Itys, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The murder of Itys is described as an act committed by Progne in a frantic fit, after which the swallow represents her restless search for her son. Homer preserves a different tradition in which Ædon mistakenly kills her son Itylus while intending to kill her nephew.

l: the nightingale, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The nightingale is said to conceal itself in woods and thickets, symbolizing the concealment of Philomela’s misfortunes and sorrows. In the alternative account of Anacreon and Apollodorus, the nightingale represents Progne rather than Philomela.

l: the swallow, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The swallow frequents human dwellings, symbolizing Progne’s restlessness as she seeks in vain for the son whom she has murdered. In the alternative account of Anacreon and Apollodorus, Philomela is transformed into the swallow instead.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Boreas seeks to marry Orithyïa, but Erectheus refuses his consent, so Boreas carries her away by force to Thrace. Boreas declares that violence suits his nature and uses his wind power to abduct Orithyïa. Orithyïa becomes Boreas's wife and gives birth to the winged twins Calaïs and Zethes. When they grow older, Calaïs and Zethes join the Minyæ in seeking the Golden Fleece aboard the first ship.

l: Boreas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Boreas seeks Orithyïa in marriage but, after Erectheus refuses his consent, abandons persuasion and carries her away by force. He uses his winds to shake the earth, ruffle the sea, sweep the ground, and fly with Orithyïa to the people and walls of the Ciconians.

l: Erectheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Erectheus is king of Athens and receives the sceptre and government of the country. He refuses to consent to Boreas's marriage with Orithyïa.

l: Orithyïa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Orithyïa is the daughter of Erectheus. Boreas carries her away while she trembles with fear, and she becomes his wife and the mother of Calaïs and Zethes.

l: Calaïs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Calaïs is born as one of the twin sons of Boreas and Orithyïa. He initially lacks feathers, but wings later grow along his sides; after reaching youth, he joins the Minyæ in seeking the Golden Fleece.

l: Zethes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Zethes is born as one of the twin sons of Boreas and Orithyïa. He initially lacks feathers, but wings later grow along his sides; after reaching youth, he joins the Minyæ in seeking the Golden Fleece.

l: Thrace, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Thrace is the region to which Boreas carries Orithyïa after abducting her. The text also says that Tereus and the Thracians were an obstacle to Boreas.

l: Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Golden Fleece is a fleece that glittered with shining hair of gold. Calaïs and Zethes later seek it with the Minyæ aboard the first ship.

l: marriage of Boreas and Orithyïa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Boreas's marriage to Orithyïa is opposed by Erectheus, who refuses his consent. Boreas therefore makes Orithyïa his wife by carrying her away to the Ciconians in Thrace.

l: the rape of Orithyïa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: After his prayers and blandishments fail, Boreas abducts Orithyïa by force. He wraps her in his tawny wings and carries her through the air to the people and walls of the Ciconians.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains that Plato treated the rape of Orithyïa as an allegory for Orithyïa being blown into the sea and drowned. Apollodorus and Pausanias instead regarded it as historical, saying that Boreas, king of Thrace, seized Orithyïa near the river Ilissus and carried her to his dominions. There she became the mother of the twins Calaïs and Zethes, who later delivered Phineus from the Harpies during the Argonautic expedition.

l: the rape of Orithyïa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Plato interpreted the story allegorically, as meaning that Orithyïa was accidentally blown by the wind into the sea and drowned. Apollodorus and Pausanias treated it as based on historical events involving Boreas's seizure of Orithyïa.

l: Orithyïa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Orithyïa was the daughter of Erectheus, king of Athens, and the sister of Procris. According to Apollodorus and Pausanias, Boreas seized her as she was passing the river Ilissus and carried her to Thrace, where she became the mother of Calaïs and Zethes.

l: Boreas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Boreas was described as the king of Thrace. According to Apollodorus and Pausanias, he seized Orithyïa near the river Ilissus and carried her into his dominions.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Jason and the Argonauts arrive in Colchis seeking the Golden Fleece from Æetes. Medea falls violently in love with Jason and uses her enchantments and enchanted herbs to protect him from the brazen-footed bulls, the Earth-born warriors, and the dragon guarding the fleece. Jason completes the required labors, obtains the Golden Fleece, and returns victoriously to Iolcos with Medea as his wife.

l: Jason, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Jason arrives in Colchis with the Argonauts and asks Æetes for the Golden Fleece. With Medea’s aid, he withstands the flames of the brazen-footed bulls, makes them plough the field, causes the Earth-born warriors to destroy one another, puts the dragon guarding the fleece to sleep, and takes the Golden Fleece. He returns victoriously to Iolcos with Medea as his wife.

l: Medea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Medea, the daughter of Æetes, falls in love with Jason and struggles between her love and her loyalty to her father and homeland. She gives Jason enchanted herbs, repeats protective charms, and helps him survive his labors; she then leaves with him and becomes his wife.

l: Argonauts, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: The Argonauts travel in the Pagasæan ship with Jason and arrive in Colchis after many adventures. They witness Jason’s success and celebrate his victory.

l: Æetes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Æetes is the king of Colchis and the father of Medea. He requires Jason to perform several dangerous labors before receiving the Golden Fleece.

l: Earth-born warriors, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: The Earth-born warriors grow from the dragon’s teeth that Jason sows in the ploughed field. They prepare to attack Jason, but he throws a stone among them, causing them to turn against one another and perish in mutual wounds.

l: dragon guarding the Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: The dragon guarding the Golden Fleece has a crest, three tongues, and hooked teeth. Medea’s herbs and words put it to sleep, allowing Jason to take the fleece.

l: brazen-footed bulls, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: The brazen-footed bulls have iron-pointed horns and breathe flames from their adamantine nostrils. Protected by Medea’s enchantments, Jason strokes them, yokes them, and makes them plough the field.

l: Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: The Golden Fleece is the prize that Jason seeks from Æetes in Colchis. After the dragon guarding it is put to sleep, Jason takes it and carries it away.

l: enchanted herbs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Medea gives Jason enchanted herbs and teaches him how to use them. The herbs protect him from the bulls’ flames and help put the dragon to sleep.

l: Medea's enchantments, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Medea’s enchantments preserve Jason from the dangers of his labors. They protect him from the bulls, aid him when the Earth-born warriors attack, and help bring sleep to the dragon.

l: Colchis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Colchis is the land where Jason and the Argonauts arrive to seek the Golden Fleece. Its king is Æetes, and its people witness Jason’s successful labors.

l: love between Medea and Jason, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Medea’s love for Jason arises when he arrives in Colchis and asks for her help. Although she recognizes the conflict between love and duty, she aids him, leaves her family and homeland with him, and becomes his wife.

l: Argonauts' voyage for the recovery of the Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Jason’s quest requires him to perform dangerous labors imposed by Æetes. With Medea’s assistance, he completes them, takes the Golden Fleece, and returns in triumph to Iolcos.

l: Jason and Medea's marriage, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SEVENTH.
s: Jason promises Medea marriage in exchange for her help, swearing by the Gods and his own adventures. After Jason obtains the Golden Fleece, he returns to Iolcos with Medea as his wife.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The unit explains the origins and legendary development of the Argonauts’ expedition to Colchis. Jason leads the Argonauts from Iolcos to recover the treasures of Athamas and avenge Phryxus, aided by Medea after she falls in love with him. It recounts the Argonauts’ earlier adventures, including their stay at Lemnos and their rescue of Phineus from the Harpies. The explanation also suggests that the Golden Fleece, fiery bulls, dragon, and dragon’s teeth may have arisen from misunderstood foreign-language accounts of treasures, defenses, and troops.

l: Argonauts, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Argonauts are the young nobles of Greece who sail with Jason in the ship Argo. During their voyage, they visit Lemnos, take wives there, rescue Phineus from the Harpies, and eventually reach Colchis.

l: Pagasæan ship, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Argo is the ship built at Pagasæ for Jason and the Argonauts. Its name is variously attributed to its speed, its builder Argus, the Argives or Greeks aboard it, or a Phœnician word meaning “long.”

l: Medea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Medea, the daughter of Æetes, falls in love with Jason and promises to help him survive the dangers of his expedition if he marries her. She gives him magical aid, conducts him to the royal palace by night, and helps him carry away the royal treasures before fleeing with him.

l: Æetes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Æetes is the king of Colchis and the kinsman of Phryxus. He causes Phryxus to be assassinated, seizes the treasures of Athamas, and establishes a custom of sacrificing strangers after receiving an oracle that a stranger will deprive him of his crown and life.

l: Jason, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jason, the son of Æson and nephew of Pelias, leads the Argonauts on their expedition to Colchis. With Medea’s assistance, he confronts the dangers set by Æetes, carries away the royal treasures, and escapes with Medea and his companions.

l: Phryxus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Phryxus, the son of Athamas and Nephele, flees with his sister Helle after Ino plots against them. He reaches Colchis, marries Chalciope, and is later assassinated by Æetes, whose death prompts the Greek expedition.

l: Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Greece supplies the noble youths who join Jason’s expedition. The Greeks undertake the voyage to recover the treasures of Athamas and avenge the death of Phryxus.

l: Iolcos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Iolcos is the Thessalian city whose throne was taken from Æson by his brother Pelias. Jason is connected with Iolcos through his family, and Pelias uses the expedition to remove him from the city.

l: Athamas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Athamas is the son of Æolus and the father of Phryxus and Helle. After Phryxus’s death, Æetes seizes Athamas’s treasures, which becomes one of the stated reasons for the Greek expedition.

l: Pelias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Pelias drives his brother Æson from the throne of Iolcos and seeks to send away Æson’s son, Jason. Because an oracle warns him to beware of a person with one shoe, he encourages Jason to undertake the dangerous expedition, expecting him to perish.

l: Colchis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Colchis is the realm ruled by Æetes and the destination of Jason and the Argonauts. Phryxus reaches Colchis and marries there, while Jason later enters it with Medea’s aid and removes Æetes’s treasures.

l: Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Golden Fleece is presented as part of the poetic version of the Argonauts’ story. The explanation suggests that it may have originated from a misunderstood account of a treasure, or from the gilt skin of the sheep sacrificed by Phryxus.

l: treasures of Athamas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The treasures of Athamas are seized by Æetes after the death of Phryxus. Recovering them and avenging Phryxus’s death are given as motives for the Greeks’ expedition, and Jason ultimately carries them away with Medea’s assistance.

l: the Argonautic expedition, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jason’s expedition is organized by Pelias and undertaken by Jason with the Argonauts to recover Athamas’s treasures and avenge Phryxus. It brings the group from Iolcos through several adventures to Colchis, where Jason receives Medea’s aid and escapes with the treasures.

l: Argonauts' voyage for the recovery of the Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The voyage of the Argonauts includes the departure from Iolcos, the stay at Lemnos, the rescue of Phineus from the Harpies, and the arrival at Colchis. The unit presents it as one of the most remarkable events of the fabulous ages and explains how later poets added its miraculous elements.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jason asks Medea to restore his aged father Æson, and Medea uses her magic, herbs, rituals, and a potion to rejuvenate him. Medea then deceives the daughters of Pelias by demonstrating that she can turn an old ram into a lamb and promising to restore their father’s youth. The daughters stab the sleeping Pelias so that Medea can replace his old blood, but Medea cuts his throat and puts his mangled body into the boiling cauldron. Medea thereby carries out her revenge against Pelias and escapes the consequences of his death.

l: Medea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Medea responds to Jason’s request by restoring Æson’s youth through elaborate magic, herbs, sacrifices, and a potion. She later deceives the daughters of Pelias, persuading them to stab their father, and completes her revenge by cutting his throat and placing his body in the cauldron.

l: Jason, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jason asks Medea to restore his aged father Æson, even offering to surrender some of his own years. Medea instead promises to renew Æson without taking years from Jason and orders Jason to remain away while she performs the rites.
